article_title: What Further Research Is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools?
citation: Hurley, N., Guckenburg, S., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). What Further Research is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools? WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: RP-Observe observation tool for measuring restorative justice in schools
description: RP-Observe is an observation tool that Rutgers University developed to measure RJ in schools, cited by experts among the very few instruments designed to measure RJ. The article reports that experts often created their own instruments, including fidelity instruments specific to the RJ model being implemented, and that some approach measurement through changes in school climate and relationships among students and staff. Interviewees agreed a resource should compile and disseminate existing evaluation tools and findings.
requirements: Sound measurement of RJ, which experts recognize is required to learn about its impact
constraints: Experts noted measuring RJ is challenging because RJ is about the overall school environment, communication, and a way of being
target_learners: K–12 students and school staff observed during RJ implementation
target_learning_goals: measuring implementation fidelity and outcomes of restorative justice practices
examples: Experts created their own fidelity instruments specific to the model of RJ being implemented
key_sources: Hurley, N., Guckenburg, S., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). What Further Research is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools? WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED559727

article_title: Curiosity: The effects of feedback and confidence on the desire to know.
citation: Metcalfe, J., Vuorre, M., Towner, E., & Eich, T. S. (2023). Curiosity: The effects of feedback and confidence on the desire to know. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, vol. 152, no. 2, pp. 464-482. https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0001284
title: Region of proximal learning (RPL) model of curiosity
description: The RPL framework holds that curiosity is minimal when people are certain they know an answer and maximal when they believe they almost know it. The article modifies the model from Metcalfe et al. (2017) with a hard knowledge boundary under definitive yes/no feedback and a soft, noisy boundary when feedback truth is uncertain. The authors state the results are "consistent with the region of proximal learning model which proposes that while curiosity is minimal when people are completely certain that they know the answer, it is maximal when people believe that they almost know."
requirements: Metaknowledge that one almost knows is described as critical and necessary for curiosity to be aroused
constraints: The model's soft-boundary predictions apply when the truth of feedback is uncertain; with definitive yes/no feedback the known/unknown boundary is hard
target_learning_goals: epistemic curiosity about specific answers to general information questions
examples: Figure 1 illustrates the model with a hard boundary (left panel) for definitive feedback and a soft boundary (right panel) for uncertain feedback
key_sources: Metcalfe, J., Vuorre, M., Towner, E., & Eich, T. S. (2023). Curiosity: The effects of feedback and confidence on the desire to know. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, vol. 152, no. 2, pp. 464-482. https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0001284

article_title: High-School Students Believe School Physics Helps in Developing Logical but Not Creative Thinking: Active Learning Can Change This Idea
citation: Mirko Marušić & Josip Sliško. (2014). High-School Students Believe School Physics Helps in Developing Logical But not Creative Thinking: Active Learning Can Change This Idea. European J of Physics Education, Volume 5 Issue 4. http://www.edpsycinteractive.org/topics/affect/humed.html
title: Reading, Presenting, and Questioning (RPQ) learning package
description: RPQ is a learning package combining a teaching method with modern-physics topics (the Large Hadron Collider at CERN and the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropic Probe), applied to three physics sections of 91 students. It comprises students' autonomous reading of popular articles and online resources, PowerPoint presentations of learning results, and questioning about unclear elements of reading and peer-presented materials, with sections broken into three teams to encourage discussion. Its rationale draws on "read to learn", "present to learn", and "question to learn" practices.
requirements: Teacher-researcher-suggested popular articles and online resources on recent scientific discoveries in physics
16 forty five-minute free-topic sessions across the semester, including sessions for pre and post assessments
target_learning_goals: perceptions of physics learning as developing logical and creative thinking
understanding of recent scientific discoveries in physics
examples: Students presented learning results in PowerPoint format and questioned unclear elements of reading and peer-presented materials
key_sources: Mirko Marušić & Josip Sliško. (2014). High-School Students Believe School Physics Helps in Developing Logical But not Creative Thinking: Active Learning Can Change This Idea. European J of Physics Education, Volume 5 Issue 4. http://www.edpsycinteractive.org/topics/affect/humed.html
